entries.meaning: A machine that presses inked type or plates onto paper to make many copies. ---
examples: The museum has a working printing press from 1850.
Gutenberg's printing press changed how books were made.
Two of the shop's printing presses run all night.

entries.meaning: A small business that prints things for customers. ---
examples: There's a print shop on the corner that does business cards.
I dropped the flyers off at the print shop this morning.
Most of the print shops downtown have closed.

entries.meaning: A copy of a document made by a machine that scans and prints it. ---
examples: Bring the original and one photocopy.
The photocopy came out too dark to read.
She kept photocopies of every receipt.

entries.meaning: An office machine that makes paper copies of documents. ---
examples: The photocopier is out of paper again.
Somebody left a whole report sitting in the photocopier.
Both photocopiers on this floor are broken.

entries.meaning: An everyday name for a photocopier. ---
examples: The copy machine is down the hall by the break room.
I need ten copies — is the copy machine working?
They replaced both copy machines last spring.

entries.meaning: A store where you can pay to copy, print, and bind documents. ---
examples: Run these off at the copy shop near campus.
The copy shop stays open until midnight during finals.
There used to be three copy shops on this street.

entries.meaning: A version of a document printed on paper rather than kept on a screen. ---
examples: Can you email it and also bring a hard copy?
The judge wants a hard copy of every exhibit.
Keep hard copies of your tax forms for seven years.

entries.meaning: A printer that fuses powdered toner onto paper with heat. ---
examples: A laser printer is cheaper to run than an inkjet.
Our laser printer prints forty pages a minute.
The office has laser printers on every floor.

entries.meaning: A printer that sprays tiny drops of liquid ink onto paper. ---
examples: An inkjet printer does a better job on photos.
My inkjet printer clogs if I don't use it for a month.
Cheap inkjet printers cost more in ink than in hardware.

entries.meaning: A small sealed container of ink that slides into a printer. ---
examples: The black ink cartridge is almost empty.
A replacement ink cartridge costs thirty dollars.
I bought a pack of four ink cartridges online.

entries.meaning: The thick colored paste used on a press to print on paper. ---
examples: The shop smells like printing ink and hot paper.
Printing ink is much stiffer than the ink in a pen.
They switched to a soy-based printing ink.

entries.meaning: The container of toner powder that fits inside a laser printer. ---
examples: Shake the toner cartridge before you put it back in.
A new toner cartridge lasts about three thousand pages.
We keep two spare toner cartridges in the closet.

entries.meaning: The part of a printer that puts the ink onto the paper. ---
examples: Run the cleaning cycle if the print head is clogged.
A dirty print head leaves streaks down the page.
Replacing the print head costs almost as much as a new printer.

entries.meaning: A stoppage caused by paper getting stuck inside a printer or copier. ---
examples: The screen says paper jam again.
Open the back panel to clear the paper jam.
We've had three paper jams this morning.

entries.meaning: The sliding drawer that holds blank paper in a printer. ---
examples: Somebody forgot to fill the paper tray.
Load the letterhead face down in the paper tray.
The printer has two paper trays for different sizes.

entries.meaning: Ordinary white paper cut to fit a home or office printer. ---
examples: Pick up some printer paper while you're out.
We're down to half a pack of printer paper.
This printer paper is too thin for double-sided printing.

entries.meaning: Plain lightweight paper made for copiers and office printers. ---
examples: The supply closet is full of copy paper.
Plain copy paper is fine for the draft.
A case of copy paper holds ten reams.

entries.meaning: Thick coated paper made for printing photographs. ---
examples: Print it on glossy photo paper.
Photo paper costs about a dollar a sheet.
The colors look flat unless you use real photo paper.

entries.meaning: Ream has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Grab a ream of paper from the closet.
A ream is five hundred sheets.
The report went through six reams of paper.
The lawsuit produced reams of paperwork.
She took reams of notes at the hearing.
There are reams of data and nobody to read it.

senses.head: A standard package of five hundred sheets of paper
examples: Grab a ream of paper from the closet.
A ream is five hundred sheets.
The report went through six reams of paper.

senses.head: A very large amount of paper or writing
examples: The lawsuit produced reams of paperwork.
She took reams of notes at the hearing.
There are reams of data and nobody to read it.

entries.русский: пачка бумаги (500 листов); кипы, горы (бумаг, записей)

entries.meaning: One batch of pages sent to a printer at a time. ---
examples: Cancel that print job before it wastes the whole tray.
My print job is stuck in the queue.
There are four print jobs ahead of yours.

entries.meaning: The number of copies printed at one time. ---
examples: The first print run was only two thousand copies.
They doubled the print run after the reviews came out.
Small print runs cost more per copy.

entries.meaning: A flat metal sheet carrying the image that a press inks and prints from. ---
examples: The printing plate is made fresh for every job.
A scratch on the printing plate shows up on every copy.
The old aluminum printing plates get recycled.

entries.meaning: A hand tool with raised rubber letters used to print a mark on paper. ---
examples: She marked the invoice PAID with a rubber stamp.
The clerk reached for his rubber stamp.
A drawer full of old rubber stamps sat by the window.

entries.meaning: A shallow box of soaked felt that you press a stamp onto. ---
examples: The ink pad has dried out.
Press the stamp on the ink pad first.
The kids got two ink pads with the stamp set.

entries.meaning: A small pot of ink that a pen is dipped into. ---
examples: The old desk still has a hole for an inkwell.
He dipped the nib in the inkwell and kept writing.
The museum displays glass inkwells from the 1800s.

entries.meaning: A board with a long hinged blade for trimming stacks of paper. ---
examples: Trim the edges on the paper cutter.
Watch your fingers on that paper cutter.
The bindery has two heavy paper cutters.
entries.contrast: American; the British normally call this a guillotine.

entries.meaning: A machine that cuts documents into thin strips so they can't be read. ---
examples: Put the old statements through the paper shredder.
The paper shredder jammed on a stapled packet.
Every desk on that floor has its own paper shredder.

entries.meaning: A factory that turns wood pulp into paper. ---
examples: His grandfather worked at the paper mill.
You can smell the paper mill from the highway.
Three paper mills in the state shut down last year.

entries.meaning: A duplicate made at the same time by writing through a sheet of carbon paper. ---
examples: Keep the yellow carbon copy for your records.
The receipt book makes a carbon copy of every sale.
She filed the carbon copies of all her letters.

entries.meaning: Thin paper coated with dark pigment that transfers writing to the sheet below. ---
examples: Slide a sheet of carbon paper between the forms.
Nobody under thirty has used carbon paper.
The carbon paper left smudges on her fingers.

entries.meaning: Thick colored paper used by children for cutting and pasting. ---
examples: The class made turkeys out of construction paper.
We need red and orange construction paper.
Construction paper fades fast in the sun.
entries.contrast: An American term; British schools call it sugar paper.

entries.meaning: Used or leftover paper kept for rough notes. ---
examples: Work it out on scrap paper first.
There's a box of scrap paper by the printer.
He wrote the address on a piece of scrap paper.

entries.meaning: Thin see-through paper used for copying a drawing by hand. ---
examples: Lay the tracing paper over the sketch.
A roll of tracing paper costs a few dollars.
The plans came with a sheet of tracing paper on top.

entries.meaning: Stiff heavy paper used for covers, cards, and invitations. ---
examples: Print the invitations on white cardstock.
The cover is heavy cardstock, not regular paper.
This cardstock is too thick for the printer.
entries.contrast: American; the British usually just say card.

entries.meaning: The cheap rough paper that newspapers are printed on. ---
examples: Newsprint turns yellow in a couple of years.
The comics were printed on gray newsprint.
The price of newsprint went up again.
entries.contrast: American NOOZ-, not the British NYOOZ-.

entries.meaning: Paper printed at the top with an organization's name and address. ---
examples: The offer came on company letterhead.
Type the reference letter on department letterhead.
We ordered new letterhead after the logo changed.

entries.meaning: The particular kind and weight of paper a job is printed on. ---
examples: The brochure needs a heavier paper stock.
They chose an uncoated paper stock for the novel.
Ask the printer what paper stock he recommends.

entries.meaning: Pulp has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The mill grinds the logs into pulp.
Recycled paper is mixed back into the pulp.
Wet pulp is pressed and dried into sheets.
I like orange juice with plenty of pulp.
Scoop the pulp out of the melon.
Strain the juice to get rid of the pulp.
He wrote detective pulp for a penny a word.
The store keeps a shelf of old pulp by the window.
Critics dismissed the novel as pulp.

senses.head: The soft wet mass of wood fiber that paper is made from
examples: The mill grinds the logs into pulp.
Recycled paper is mixed back into the pulp.
Wet pulp is pressed and dried into sheets.

senses.head: The soft juicy part of a fruit or vegetable
examples: I like orange juice with plenty of pulp.
Scoop the pulp out of the melon.
Strain the juice to get rid of the pulp.

senses.head: Cheap sensational fiction, originally printed on rough paper
examples: He wrote detective pulp for a penny a word.
The store keeps a shelf of old pulp by the window.
Critics dismissed the novel as pulp.

entries.русский: бумажная масса, целлюлоза; мякоть (плода); бульварное чтиво

entries.meaning: Fine smooth writing material, originally calfskin and now a heavy translucent paper. ---
examples: The medieval manuscript was written on vellum.
The invitations came wrapped in a sheet of vellum.
Vellum has a slightly waxy feel.

entries.meaning: The page at the front of a book giving its title, author, and publisher. ---
examples: He signed the book on the title page.
The title page lists both translators.
Early editions have very plain title pages.

entries.meaning: The list at the front of a book showing chapters and their page numbers. ---
examples: Check the table of contents for the chapter on grammar.
The table of contents runs three pages.
Textbooks usually have detailed tables of contents.
entries.contrast: Plural is tables of contents — the s moves to table, not to contents.

entries.meaning: The page at the front of a book listing the publisher, date, and legal notices. ---
examples: The printing history is on the copyright page.
You can tell it's a first edition from the copyright page.
Nobody reads copyright pages except collectors.
entries.русский: оборот титульного листа, страница с выходными данными

entries.meaning: The outside face at the beginning of a book or magazine. ---
examples: Her name is right on the front cover.
The front cover is scuffed but the pages are clean.
All four front covers used the same photograph.

entries.meaning: The outside face at the end of a book or magazine. ---
examples: The blurbs are printed on the back cover.
The price is in the corner of the back cover.
Magazine back covers sell for a lot in advertising.

entries.meaning: The stiff outer part that protects the pages of a book. ---
examples: Don't judge a book cover by the color.
The book cover was designed by an artist in Brooklyn.
The library reinforces its book covers with clear tape.

entries.meaning: The loose paper wrapper that slips over a hardcover book. ---
examples: The dust jacket is torn at the top.
A first edition is worth much more with its dust jacket.
He takes the dust jackets off before he reads.

entries.meaning: The figure printed on a page to show its place in the book. ---
examples: Give me the page number so I can find the quote.
The page number sits in the outer corner.
The page numbers start over in the appendix.

entries.meaning: The total number of pages in a document or book. ---
examples: We need to cut the page count by fifty.
A higher page count means a higher printing bill.
The two editions have very different page counts.

entries.meaning: A page with nothing printed on it. ---
examples: There's a blank page between the chapters.
Nothing is scarier than a blank page.
The printer spat out six blank pages.

entries.meaning: The page opposite the one you are reading in an open book. ---
examples: The map is on the facing page.
The translation runs on the facing page.
The photographs and captions sit on facing pages.

entries.meaning: A blank leaf at the very front or back of a bound book. ---
examples: Her grandmother's name was written on the flyleaf.
He jotted the date on the flyleaf.
Someone had torn out both flyleaves.
entries.русский: форзацный лист (чистый лист в начале книги)
entries.contrast: Irregular plural: flyleaves, not flyleafs.

entries.meaning: The sheet glued between a book's cover and its first or last page. ---
examples: The endpaper is printed with a map of the island.
Glue had stained the endpaper brown.
The atlas has marbled endpapers.

entries.meaning: A small printed label pasted inside a book to show who owns it. ---
examples: There's a bookplate from the old town library inside.
He had a bookplate made with his initials on it.
Collectors trade antique bookplates.

entries.meaning: An illustration facing the title page of a book. ---
examples: The frontispiece is a portrait of the author.
An engraved frontispiece opens the volume.
Both frontispieces were printed from the same plate.
entries.contrast: Not front-is-piece: the first syllable sounds like front — FRUN-tuh-spees.

entries.meaning: A note or emblem in a book giving details about how it was made. ---
examples: The colophon names the typeface and the paper.
The publisher's colophon is a little sailing ship.
Fine presses print elaborate colophons.
entries.contrast: Stress the first syllable: KAH-luh-fuhn, not kuh-LOH-fahn.

entries.meaning: A large book made from sheets folded once, or a sheet folded that way. ---
examples: The library owns a Shakespeare folio.
The atlas is a heavy leather folio.
Rare folios are kept in a locked case.

entries.meaning: The right-hand page of an open book, or the front of a leaf. ---
examples: Every chapter opens on a recto.
The illustration is printed on the recto.
Odd page numbers always fall on rectos.

entries.meaning: The left-hand page of an open book, or the back of a leaf. ---
examples: The copyright notice sits on the verso of the title page.
Nothing is printed on the verso.
Even numbers land on the versos.

entries.meaning: The craft of fastening printed pages together inside covers. ---
examples: She takes a class in bookbinding on Saturdays.
Bookbinding by hand takes years to learn.
The shop still does traditional bookbinding.

entries.meaning: A workshop where printed sheets are folded, sewn, and bound into books. ---
examples: The sheets go from the press to the bindery.
The bindery runs a second shift in the fall.
Only a few binderies still sew by hand.

entries.meaning: A way of holding pages together with a coil of wire or plastic through punched holes. ---
examples: Ask for spiral binding so it lies flat.
The cookbook has spiral binding.
Spiral binding costs three dollars extra.

entries.meaning: A binding method in which the pages are glued at the spine instead of sewn. ---
examples: Most paperbacks use perfect binding.
Perfect binding is cheap but the spine can crack.
The printer quoted us for perfect binding.

entries.meaning: A book bound in flexible paper covers rather than boards. ---
examples: The softcover comes out in the spring.
I'd rather carry a softcover on the plane.
The publisher printed both hardcovers and softcovers.

entries.meaning: The rough untrimmed edge left on a sheet of handmade or fine paper. ---
examples: The pages have a deckle edge on the outside.
A deckle edge makes the book feel handmade.
The stationery came with soft deckle edges.

entries.meaning: The art of arranging printed letters so text looks right and reads well. ---
examples: The typography on that poster is beautiful.
He teaches typography at the art school.
Good typography is invisible to most readers.
entries.contrast: Stress the second syllable: ty-PAH-gruh-fee.

entries.meaning: The work of arranging text into lines and pages ready for printing. ---
examples: The typesetting took two weeks.
Computers replaced hot-metal typesetting.
There are still errors from the typesetting.

entries.meaning: A person who sets text into type for printing. ---
examples: The typesetter caught the mistake before we did.
His father was a typesetter at the paper.
The union protected the typesetters for years.

entries.meaning: Type has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The book is set in ten-point type.
The type is too small for me to read comfortably.
Old presses printed from metal type.
What type of car does she drive?
This type of soil holds water well.
The store carries three types of batteries.

senses.head: Printed letters and characters considered as a whole
examples: The book is set in ten-point type.
The type is too small for me to read comfortably.
Old presses printed from metal type.

senses.head: A kind or category of person or thing
examples: What type of car does she drive?
This type of soil holds water well.
The store carries three types of batteries.

entries.meaning: Separate metal letters that can be arranged, printed, and used again. ---
examples: Movable type made cheap books possible.
The shop still prints with movable type.
Each letter of movable type was cast by hand.

entries.meaning: A small finishing stroke at the end of a letter's main line. ---
examples: Look at the tiny serif at the foot of the letter.
This font has a very sharp serif.
Screens used to blur fine serifs.

entries.meaning: A typeface whose letters have no small finishing strokes. ---
examples: Set the headings in a clean sans serif.
Helvetica is the best-known sans serif.
Road signs use sans serifs because they read faster.
entries.contrast: From French: the s of sans is silent — san-SEH-rif, not sanz.

entries.meaning: A slanted style of type used for emphasis or for titles. ---
examples: Book titles go in italics.
Put the foreign words in italics.
He uses italics far too often.
entries.contrast: Nearly always used in the plural: in italics, not in italic.

entries.meaning: How large the printed letters are. ---
examples: Bump the font size up to twelve.
The font size on the label is impossible to read.
Try one of the larger font sizes.

entries.meaning: A set of related typefaces sharing one design in different weights and styles. ---
examples: The whole report uses a single font family.
That font family includes nine weights.
Mixing three font families on one page looks messy.

entries.meaning: The height of type measured in points. ---
examples: The body text is set at a point size of eleven.
Check the point size before you send it to print.
Large-print books use much bigger point sizes.

entries.meaning: The adjustment of space between two individual letters. ---
examples: The kerning on that sign is terrible.
Designers argue about kerning for hours.
Fix the kerning between the A and the V.

entries.meaning: The vertical space between lines of type. ---
examples: Open up the leading so the page breathes.
Tight leading makes long text hard to read.
The leading is set two points above the type size.
entries.contrast: Rhymes with wedding, not with reading — the name comes from strips of lead.

entries.meaning: Two or more letters joined into a single printed character. ---
examples: The f and the i form a ligature.
This typeface has a lovely ligature.
Old books are full of ligatures.

entries.meaning: A single printed shape for a letter, number, or symbol. ---
examples: The font is missing a glyph for that symbol.
Each glyph is drawn on a grid.
The typeface ships with two thousand glyphs.

entries.meaning: The part of a lowercase letter that rises above the main body, as in b or d. ---
examples: The letter h has a tall ascender.
Shorten the ascender and the font looks cramped.
The ascenders almost touch the line above.

entries.meaning: The part of a lowercase letter that drops below the line, as in g or p. ---
examples: The tail of the y is its descender.
The descender gets cut off in this box.
Long descenders need extra space between lines.

entries.meaning: The height of a lowercase letter without its rising or falling parts. ---
examples: This face has a large x-height, so it reads well small.
Compare the x-height of the two fonts.
Fonts with tiny x-heights look elegant but faint.

entries.meaning: The invisible line that letters sit on. ---
examples: The o dips slightly below the baseline.
Align the caption to the baseline of the text.
The two columns share the same baselines.

entries.meaning: A large opening letter set down into the first lines of a paragraph. ---
examples: Each chapter starts with a drop cap.
The drop cap runs three lines deep.
Old printed books used decorated drop caps.

entries.meaning: A large form of a letter used to begin a sentence or a name. ---
examples: Start the sentence with a capital letter.
The sign was painted in one huge capital letter.
Fill out the form in capital letters.

entries.meaning: The amount of blank room left between lines of text. ---
examples: The professor wants double line spacing.
Tighten the line spacing to save a page.
The line spacing makes the essay look padded.

entries.meaning: The empty area on a page around text and pictures. ---
examples: The layout needs more white space.
Don't be afraid of white space on the cover.
Cheap ads cram every inch and leave no white space.

entries.meaning: The spacing of words so lines end evenly at both margins. ---
examples: Turn off justification and use a ragged right edge.
Bad justification leaves rivers of white down the column.
Justification works better with hyphens turned on.

entries.meaning: The breaking of words with a hyphen at the end of a line. ---
examples: Turn on hyphenation for narrow columns.
The hyphenation split the name in a strange place.
Newspapers rely on hyphenation to fill their lines.

entries.meaning: The point where one line of text ends and the next begins. ---
examples: Put a line break after the address.
That line break falls in an awkward spot.
The poem's line breaks change the whole rhythm.

entries.meaning: The point where text stops on one page and continues on the next. ---
examples: Insert a page break before the appendix.
The table got split by a page break.
Check all the page breaks before printing.

entries.meaning: Header has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Put the chapter title in the header.
The header shows the date on every page.
The two sections use different headers.
She scored on a header from six yards out.
His header went just over the crossbar.
The goalie punched away two dangerous headers.
He took a header off his bike and split his lip.
The waiter tripped on the rug and took a header.
One wrong step on that ladder and you'll take a header.

senses.head: A line of text repeated at the top of every page
examples: Put the chapter title in the header.
The header shows the date on every page.
The two sections use different headers.

senses.head: In soccer, a shot or pass made by hitting the ball with the head
examples: She scored on a header from six yards out.
His header went just over the crossbar.
The goalie punched away two dangerous headers.

senses.head: A fall or dive headfirst
examples: He took a header off his bike and split his lip.
The waiter tripped on the rug and took a header.
One wrong step on that ladder and you'll take a header.

entries.русский: верхний колонтитул; удар головой (в футболе); падение головой вперёд

entries.meaning: A line of text repeated at the bottom of every page. ---
examples: The page number goes in the footer.
Add the file name to the footer.
The footers fell off the last two pages.

entries.meaning: A small heading that breaks a long article into sections. ---
examples: Add a subhead every few paragraphs.
The subhead gives away the ending.
Readers skim the subheads before they commit.

entries.meaning: The printed box in a paper or magazine listing its editors and publisher. ---
examples: Her name is finally on the masthead.
Check the masthead to see who owns the paper.
Half the mastheads in town got shorter this year.
entries.contrast: In American use the masthead is the staff list; the British often mean the paper's name banner.

entries.meaning: The large picture or spread printed across the middle pages of a magazine. ---
examples: The centerfold is a photo of the whole team.
He tore out the centerfold and taped it up.
The magazine's centerfolds were always maps.
entries.contrast: American spelling center-; the British write centrefold.

entries.meaning: Printing done by pressing paper against raised inked type. ---
examples: The wedding invitations were done in letterpress.
Letterpress leaves a slight dent you can feel.
She learned letterpress at a studio in Portland.

entries.meaning: Commercial printing in which ink goes from a plate to a rubber blanket and then to the paper. ---
examples: Most magazines are made by offset printing.
Offset printing gets cheap once you pass a thousand copies.
The plant does offset printing around the clock.

entries.meaning: Printing by pushing ink through a stencil stretched on fine mesh. ---
examples: The T-shirts were done with screen printing.
Screen printing lays down thick, bright color.
He runs a screen printing business out of his garage.

entries.meaning: Printing from a flat stone or plate on which greasy ink sticks only to the drawn image. ---
examples: The posters were made by lithography.
Lithography was invented at the end of the 1700s.
She studied lithography for two semesters.
entries.contrast: Stress the second syllable: lih-THAH-gruh-fee.

entries.meaning: The process of cutting a design into metal with acid, or a print made that way. ---
examples: A small etching hangs above the desk.
He learned etching from his teacher in Chicago.
The gallery sells signed etchings.
entries.countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings

entries.meaning: A print made from a design carved into a block of wood. ---
examples: The chapter opens with a woodcut of a ship.
Each woodcut is printed by hand.
The book is illustrated with Japanese woodcuts.

entries.meaning: A person who cuts images or letters into metal or wood for printing. ---
examples: The engraver signed the plate in the corner.
A skilled engraver could copy any painting.
The mint employs a handful of engravers.

entries.meaning: The art of making pictures by printing them from a block, plate, or screen. ---
examples: She majored in printmaking.
The studio has a whole room for printmaking.
Printmaking lets an artist sell many originals.

entries.meaning: A printed picture built from tiny dots that imitate shades of gray. ---
examples: Under a magnifier the photo is just a halftone.
The halftone looks muddy on newsprint.
Old newspapers printed coarse halftones.
entries.contrast: The l of half stays silent: HAF-tohn.

entries.meaning: A faint design pressed into paper that shows when you hold it to the light. ---
examples: Hold the bill up and look for the watermark.
The stationery has the school's watermark.
Forgers have trouble with watermarks.

entries.meaning: The pressing of a raised design into paper or a cover. ---
examples: The title is done in gold embossing.
Embossing adds about a dollar per copy.
You can feel the embossing with your thumb.

entries.meaning: A thin plastic coating sealed onto paper to protect it. ---
examples: The menus have a heavy lamination.
Lamination keeps the cards from tearing.
The cover has a matte lamination.

entries.meaning: Producing printed material with page-layout software on a personal computer. ---
examples: Desktop publishing put a print shop on every desk.
She took a night class in desktop publishing.
The newsletter is done with basic desktop publishing.

entries.meaning: A company that produces and sells books or magazines. ---
examples: A small publishing house in Boston took the book.
The publishing house was founded in 1912.
Five publishing houses control most of the market.

entries.meaning: A publisher owned by a university that puts out scholarly books. ---
examples: Her dissertation was picked up by a university press.
A university press rarely pays much of an advance.
Several university presses have cut their lists.

entries.meaning: A tiny independent publisher that brings out only a few books a year. ---
examples: The poems came out from a small press in Iowa.
A small press can take risks the big houses won't.
Small presses live off grants and volunteers.

entries.meaning: A publisher that prints a book only if the author pays for it. ---
examples: He finally gave up and went to a vanity press.
A vanity press will print anything you pay for.
Reviewers ignore books from vanity presses.

entries.meaning: Bringing out your own book without a publishing company. ---
examples: Self-publishing has lost most of its old stigma.
She made more from self-publishing than from her contract.
Self-publishing means you handle the marketing yourself.

entries.meaning: A system that prints a single copy of a book only after someone orders it. ---
examples: The title is available through print-on-demand.
Print-on-demand means no warehouse full of unsold books.
Out-of-print classics have come back through print-on-demand.

entries.meaning: Newspapers and magazines taken together, as opposed to radio, TV, and the internet. ---
examples: Ad money keeps draining out of print media.
She spent thirty years in print media.
Print media still breaks most of the big stories.

entries.meaning: A version of a book or magazine meant to be read on a screen. ---
examples: The digital edition comes free with a subscription.
The digital edition has extra photographs.
Digital editions now outsell paper for that title.

entries.meaning: A copy from the first batch of a book ever printed. ---
examples: This is a signed first edition.
The first edition had a different cover.
He collects first editions of American novels.

entries.meaning: A printing of a fixed small number of numbered copies. ---
examples: It came out as a limited edition of five hundred.
My copy of the limited edition is number twelve.
Limited editions sell out before the reviews appear.
